title: Milestone: The High Middle Ages
objective: After this level you can connect feudalism, the Church and the Crusades into one picture of medieval Europe.
summary: From 1095 to 1291 the Crusades filled two centuries of the high Middle Ages and drew Rome’s three heirs into one story that also struck Jews and Christian Constantinople.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Let’s put the Crusades in one picture.
cards.body: From a pope’s speech in 1095 to the fall of Acre in 1291, crusading in the Holy Land lasted almost two centuries. Here’s how it fits the Middle Ages you met in Level 1.

events.label: Urban II calls for a crusade at Clermont

cards.headline: Rome’s heirs, meeting again
cards.body: Level 1 split the Middle Ages into early, high and late. The Crusades, from 1095 to 1291, sit in the high Middle Ages, between the early period (to about 1000) and the late one (from about 1300). Remember Level 10’s three heirs of Rome? The Crusades pulled all three into one story: a Byzantine emperor asked the pope in the West for help against Muslim Turks. Along the way, crusaders also attacked the Rhineland’s Jewish communities in 1096 and sacked Christian Constantinople in 1204. It was never a simple two-sided war.

mascot.line: Ten levels, three heirs of Rome, two centuries. That’s a milestone well earned.

cards.headline: Milestone: the Crusades in one picture
learned: Why a Byzantine plea for help against the Turks became two centuries of crusading in the Holy Land.
How divided Muslim rivals helped the crusaders take Jerusalem, and how Saladin united them to win it back.
Why the Fourth Crusade, deep in debt to Venice, ended up sacking Christian Constantinople.
What the Crusades changed: richer Italian trading cities, embittered Greeks and long memories on all sides.

questions.prompt: Crusades milestone: which order of events is right?

options.label: Crusaders take Jerusalem, Saladin retakes it, crusaders sack Constantinople
Saladin takes Jerusalem, crusaders sack Constantinople, crusaders take Jerusalem
options.rationale: The crusaders took Jerusalem first, in 1099.

options.label: Crusaders sack Constantinople, crusaders take Jerusalem, Saladin retakes it
Crusaders take Jerusalem, crusaders sack Constantinople, Saladin retakes it

questions.prompt: When the Knights Templar were founded around 1120, whom did they vow to protect?

options.label: The pope in Rome
options.rationale: They served in the Holy Land.

options.label: The Byzantine emperor
options.rationale: They were a Latin order in Jerusalem.

options.label: Pilgrims traveling to the Holy Land
Merchants of Venice

questions.explanation: Hugh de Payns and eight or nine French knights vowed to protect pilgrims traveling to the Holy Land.

questions.prompt: In Level 1’s three slices of the Middle Ages, where do the Crusades of 1095 to 1291 fall?

options.label: In the early Middle Ages
In the high Middle Ages
In the late Middle Ages
After the Middle Ages ended

questions.explanation: The Crusades fall between the early period (to about 1000) and the late period (from about 1300): the high Middle Ages.

questions.prompt: Why is “Christians against Muslims” too simple a summary of the Crusades?

options.label: No Muslims took part in the fighting
The crusaders never reached the Holy Land
The popes opposed every crusade
Crusaders also attacked Jews and sacked Christian Constantinople

questions.explanation: Crusaders massacred Rhineland Jewish communities in 1096 and sacked Christian Constantinople in 1204.

questions.prompt: After Zara, what drew the Fourth Crusade to Constantinople?

options.label: An exiled prince’s promise of money and help
An order from Saladin
A call for help from Templars there
A storm that wrecked the fleet there

questions.explanation: An exiled Byzantine prince, Alexius, promised a huge payment, church submission to Rome and help on crusade if they put him on the throne.

questions.prompt: The Crusades pulled Level 10’s three heirs of Rome into one story. Which three?

options.label: Rome, Carthage and Persia
The Franks, the Vikings and the Normans
The Latin West, Byzantium and the Islamic world
England, France and the Holy Roman Empire

questions.explanation: Rome’s world passed to western kingdoms, the Byzantine Empire and the caliphate; a Byzantine appeal to the pope against Muslim Turks drew all three in.

questions.prompt: What happened in 1204 to Hagia Sophia, the church Justinian built in Level 5?

options.label: It was burned to the ground
It was looted and became a Roman Catholic cathedral
It was turned into a mosque
It was shipped in pieces to Venice

questions.explanation: Crusaders looted Hagia Sophia in 1204, and it served as a Roman Catholic cathedral until 1261.
